message.reasoning:
I am evaluating a trade offer in Monopoly.

The offer swaps NEW_YORK_AVENUE for $130 and KENTUCKY_AVENUE. I currently hold a complete yellow set and cash. The opponent controls all four railroads.

The opponent already owns St. James Place and Tennessee Avenue, so completing the orange set with New York would give them a full monopoly. Their cash is $553.

The opponent would have $423 after the trade. Player 2 holds a pink set, utilities, and a red set. Player 3 has a light blue monopoly with hotels and a green set missing North Carolina. The bank still owns Mediterranean Avenue and North Carolina Avenue.

I have a strict policy against selling New York or Park Place. Completing the opponent's orange or dark blue monopolies would be too dangerous. Player 3's light-blue hotels are extremely valuable. This trade is exactly what I rejected twice before. I am now reconsidering whether $130 and Kentucky could ever justify giving up New York.

The opponent could mortgage all four railroads for $400. Combined with their cash, they would have $823 to build eight houses immediately on the orange set. New York Avenue would rent $850 with three houses. This creates a second lethal monopoly alongside Player 3's light blue hotels.

The trade would leave me with $730 cash. Kentucky Avenue is worthless as a trade chip because the red set is split three ways. I cannot afford to build yellow houses safely. Three houses on the yellow set cost $1350, and even with the extra cash, one house would leave only $580, breaking my $600 Connecticut hotel buffer. I would be handing the opponent a complete orange monopoly while losing the orange blocker.

I will reject the offer. No counter trade is viable because New York Avenue must stay in my hand to block the opponent's orange monopoly.
